To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“We found a correspondence between neural responses in human superior temporal gyrus and structural properties of ASRs’ phonetic models.

the human and machine solutions for speech recognition are related, as revealed by a correspondence between the neural response patterns in temporal cortex and the machine-derived phonetic models, and that the human and ASR systems are related to the problem of mapping speech to words.

“We have demonstrated the potential of using ASR-derived phonemic models to predict the neural responses to speech in human superior temporal gyrus, providing a new framework for relating human and machine solutions to problems of human cognition”.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between the human and machine solutions to problems of speech recognition.
relating dynamic brain states to the dynamic machine states that support speech recognition, and with relating the neural computations supporting human speech comprehension to those that support ASR.
the relationship between human and machine solutions to a complex problem, in this case speech recognition, and aims to provide new insights into the neurobiology of human speech perception.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study demonstrates the feasibility of relating complex computations in human speech processing to the rapidly evolving speech recognition systems that address the very same problem domain.

this research demonstrates the feasibility of relating the neural computations that underpin human speech comprehension to those that underpin automatic speech recognition, by comparing the time-varying patterns of neural activity generated by the human brain as it responds to continuous speech, and the time-varyingly defined machine states that underlie the ASR analysis.
this research demonstrates the feasibility of relating the neural basis of speech recognition in humans to the computational basis of the same process in ASR systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human brain and machine solutions for speech recognition have similar properties.
the brain is not a machine, but that it can sometimes be understood as one.

we have shown that the brain and a machine can be compared in their response to the same input, and we have demonstrated the feasibility of relating the neural response to a machine-derived representation of the speech input.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we have demonstrated that the brain uses a very similar solution to the speech recognition as ASR systems.

the human brain is capable of extracting regularities from the speech signal that are similar to those extracted by the speech recognizer, but the brain does not use exactly the same regularities as the speech recognizer.
the brain and machine can be related in the same way as they relate to their respective environments, and that this relationship is not only possible, but also very useful.
